qs.q: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is caused by deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase. The classic triad is
o: Photosensitive blistering skin rash, hepatosplenomegaly, anemia
Abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and dark urine (no skin rash)
Peripheral neuropathy, renal failure, and hypertension
qs.e: AIP: autosomal dominant, porphyrin precursors (ALA, PBG) accumulate in urine. Classic triad: severe colicky abdominal pain + neuropsychiatric features (psychosis, neuropathy) + dark/port-wine urine. NO photosensitivity (unlike porphyria cutanea tarda). Precipitated by: alcohol, drugs (OCP, barbiturates, sulfonamides), fasting, infection. Treatment: IV hemin + glucose loading + avoid triggers.

qs.q: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) presents with the classic triad of
o: Abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and dark urine — WITHOUT skin involvement
Blistering photosensitive rash, hepatosplenomegaly, and hemolytic anemia
Peripheral neuropathy, renal failure, and hypertension
qs.e: AIP: porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency → ALA and PBG accumulate. No photosensitivity (porphyrins don't accumulate in skin). Precipitants: alcohol, OCP, barbiturates, sulfonamides, fasting, infection. Urine turns dark/port-wine on standing. Diagnosis: elevated urine PBG during attack. Treatment: IV hemin (heme arginate) + IV glucose (suppresses ALA synthase) + avoid triggers.

ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is a hereditary defect in hepatic heme synthesis causing neurovisceral attacks triggered by drugs, fasting, or infection. Diagnosis relies on elevated urinary porphobilinogen and porphyrins; treatment is carbohydrate loading and IV heme.

sections.p: AIP is an autosomal‑dominant disorder of the third enzyme in the heme pathway, porphobilinogen deaminase. It presents with episodic abdominal pain, constipation, neuropsychiatric changes, and peripheral weakness.
b: Prevalence: ~1/20 000 in Europe, under‑diagnosed in low‑resource settings

sections.p: Heme synthesis occurs partly in mitochondria (first and last steps) and partly in the cytosol. Porphobilinogen deaminase converts porphobilinogen (PBG) to hydroxymethylbilane; loss of activity leads to PBG accumulation.
b: Normal pathway: Glycine + Succinyl‑CoA → δ‑ALA → PBG → hydroxymethylbilane → uroporphyrinogen III → coproporphyrinogen III → protoporphyrin IX → heme

sections.p: Heme provides negative feedback on ALA synthase, the rate‑limiting enzyme. When heme is low, ALA synthase is up‑regulated, worsening PBG build‑up in AIP.
b: Triggers: drugs (e.g., barbiturates, sulfonamides), fasting, hormonal changes, infections

sections.p: Deficient porphobilinogen deaminase causes excess PBG and ALA, neurotoxic metabolites that irritate the autonomic nervous system and peripheral nerves.
b: Neurovisceral pain from autonomic ganglia irritation
Peripheral motor neuropathy, can progress to respiratory failure

sections.p: Acute attacks can be life‑threatening; early recognition avoids unnecessary surgery and guides specific therapy. Low‑resource hospitals must rely on clinical clues and simple urine tests.
b: Key triad: abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric signs, precipitating drug or fasting
Urine darkens on standing (port wine) due to oxidized porphyrins

t.b: Does the patient have excess PBG? Positive rapid test confirms an acute porphyria; if unavailable, send urine for quantitative porphyrin analysis.
Is hyponatremia present? Low Na worsens seizures; correct cautiously.
Assess hepatic involvement; mild elevation is common but severe rise suggests alternative diagnosis.

sections.p: Focus on the metabolic block, triggers, and the specific emergency treatment. Remember that AIP does NOT cause photosensitivity—unlike cutaneous porphyrias.
b: Do NOT give porphyrin‑inducing drugs (e.g., barbiturates, phenytoin).
High‑carbohydrate (≥300 g/day) and IV heme (heme arginate or hematin) are first‑line.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with vomiting and no surgical cause
Rapidly worsening weakness or respiratory compromise

faq.q: Why does fasting trigger an attack?
faq.a: Fasting induces ALA synthase, increasing ALA and PBG production, which accumulate because the downstream enzyme is deficient.

faq.q: Can AIP be diagnosed with a blood test?
faq.a: The definitive test is urinary PBG; plasma ALA may be elevated but is less specific.
Yes, it is autosomal‑dominant with low penetrance; family members may be asymptomatic carriers.

exam: Explain the biochemical block in AIP and why it leads to neurovisceral symptoms.
